ai.definition: Direct-to-Device Satellite IoT is a system where small satellites in Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) communicate directly with ground-based sensors or mobile phones, enabling data transmission without the need for intermediate ground stations.
ai.howItWorks: Satellites in LEO orbit at altitudes between 160 and 2,000 kilometers, providing a wide coverage area. They relay short, low-power messages from unmodified or lightly modified devices to other satellites or directly to Earth-based receivers, extending connectivity to remote areas such as oceans, deserts, and rural regions.
ai.problemSolved: Addressing the limitations of traditional satellite communication systems by reducing dependency on ground infrastructure, thus enhancing coverage in remote locations and providing reliable data transmission for applications like asset tracking and environmental monitoring.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves designing and building small satellites (CubeSats or smaller) capable of handling low-power communications. Components such as solar panels, batteries, communication antennas, and microcontrollers are assembled to ensure robust performance in space conditions.
ai.buildProcess: Satellites undergo rigorous testing for thermal, vibration, and electromagnetic compatibility before launch. The build process includes component selection, assembly, integration, and final testing to meet the stringent requirements of LEO operations.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include satellite development, launch expenses (ranging from $10 million to $50 million per satellite), ground station infrastructure, and ongoing operational costs for maintaining and updating the network.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is currently in a pilot phase with limited deployment, focusing on proof-of-concept demonstrations and initial market validation. Future stages may include expansion to commercial applications and scaling of operations.
ai.regulation: Regulations vary by country but generally require compliance with international space laws and agreements such as the Outer Space Treaty. Specific licensing for satellite communications and launch activities is necessary in most jurisdictions.
ai.risks: Technical risks include signal interference, data security vulnerabilities, and potential failure due to space debris or natural phenomena. Regulatory risks involve navigating complex legal frameworks and ensuring compliance with evolving standards.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain given the high initial investment and limited current market scale. Potential for growth in remote sensing, maritime tracking, and disaster response applications could drive profitability in the future.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may focus on improving satellite payload capabilities, enhancing data transmission speeds, and expanding network coverage to include more diverse use cases such as environmental monitoring and emergency communications.

glossary.def: Orbiting at altitudes between approximately 160 and 2,000 kilometers, providing a wide coverage area for satellite communication.
Small satellites typically measuring 10 cm x 10 cm x 10 cm, used in LEO for various applications including IoT communications.

subsystems.name: Satellite payload
subsystems.role: receives very faint signals from small, low-power devices and relays or processes them.

subsystems.name: Spacecraft bus and constellation
subsystems.role: keeps the payload pointed and supplies power across a fleet of satellites.
parts: orbital planes in low Earth orbit

subsystems.name: Ground segment
subsystems.role: connects the satellites to terrestrial networks.

subsystems.name: Device and radio link
subsystems.role: the sensor or handset at the far end of a very long, very lossy path.

subsystems.name: Core network and service layer
subsystems.role: makes satellites look like a normal mobile network to apps and operators.

subsystems.name: Spectrum and regulatory layer
subsystems.role: lets satellites and terrestrial networks share scarce frequencies.

buildSteps.title: Plan the link budget
buildSteps.detail: Engineers calculate whether a milliwatt transmitter in a sensor can be heard from 500–2,000 km away, which sets antenna size, altitude and data rate — usually just a few hundred bits per second per device.

buildSteps.title: Design the payload
buildSteps.detail: A large flat phased-array antenna is built from many small radiating elements so the satellite can form and steer multiple narrow beams and track fast-moving ground devices.

buildSteps.title: Build and qualify the spacecraft
buildSteps.detail: The bus and payload are integrated and shaken, baked in thermal vacuum and blasted with radio noise to prove they survive launch and the space environment.

buildSteps.title: Mass-produce the fleet
buildSteps.detail: Satellites are assembled on production lines in flat, stackable form so dozens can launch on one rocket, driving unit cost down.

buildSteps.title: Launch and raise orbit
buildSteps.detail: Rockets deploy the satellites into several orbital planes; propulsion spreads them out so coverage is continuous.

buildSteps.title: Deploy gateways and core network
buildSteps.detail: Ground stations are built where licensed spectrum and fibre backhaul are available, then connected into a mobile core.

buildSteps.title: Integrate devices and handset firmware
buildSteps.detail: Modems adopt the satellite standard and are tuned to pre-compensate for Doppler shift and the long round-trip delay.

buildSteps.title: Trial, then commercialise
buildSteps.detail: Field trials with asset trackers, agricultural sensors and emergency-messaging handsets verify coverage before paid service begins.

prerequisites.why: 3GPP Release 17 defined how satellites and terrestrial networks share a common air interface, so chipsets can serve both.
hundreds of satellites are needed for continuous coverage, which only works if each one costs far less than a traditional telecom satellite.
the antenna gain is what closes the link to a phone or sensor; large arrays are demonstrated but still being scaled.
constellations must be replenished; rideshare and reusable rockets make that affordable.
terrestrial NB-IoT and LoRa silicon is the base that satellite variants build on.
a satellite footprint crosses many countries, and each national regulator must permit the service.

pathway.milestone: established narrowband satellite messaging services alongside pilot direct-to-phone systems
pathway.unlocks: tracking of ships, livestock, containers and pipelines where no cellular coverage exists.

pathway.milestone: commercial direct-to-handset messaging and emergency SOS from ordinary phones
pathway.unlocks: coverage in dead zones for consumers and field workers without special hardware.

pathway.milestone: direct-to-device voice and low-rate data at scale through dedicated satellite fleets
pathway.unlocks: a second path to connectivity that bypasses local towers entirely.

pathway.milestone: satellite and terrestrial networks merged into one seamless core
pathway.unlocks: devices that switch between tower and satellite without the user noticing, and truly global low-power sensing.
